title: Byzantine Anatolia
subtitle: 867–1071 · The Macedonian Recovery, the Great Estates, the Cappadocian Churches and Manzikert

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Basil I to Basil II, the Anatolian generals who became emperors and the dynasty's heirs down to Romanos Diogenes

entries.label: Basil I
entries.hint: Basil, a peasant from Macedonia who rose from the stables to be co-emperor, murdered Michael III in 867 and founded the dynasty that held the throne for nearly two centuries. He destroyed the Paulician state of Tephrike, rebuilt the fleet, made a law code and brought back Byzantine campaigns in the East.
entries.note: Theophanes Continuatus 5 (Vita Basilii); Genesios; Warren Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997).

entries.label: Leo VI the Wise
entries.hint: Leo VI, a scholar-emperor and author of sermons, hymns and a military handbook, completed the Basilika, a 60-book law code in Greek, and legislated a hundred and thirteen Novels. He married four times, in defiance of the church, to secure an heir. He lost ground to the Bulgars under Symeon.
entries.note: Leo VI, Novels; Taktika; Book of the Eparch; Shaun Tougher, The Reign of Leo VI (1997).

entries.label: Romanos I Lekapenos
entries.hint: Romanos, an Armenian admiral, took the regency of the child Constantine VII and made himself emperor. He kept the empire steady in a time of Bulgarian pressure and famine and gave the East to John Kourkouas, who took Melitene in 934 and brought the Mandylion of Edessa to Constantinople in 944. His sons deposed him.
entries.note: Theophanes Continuatus 6; Skylitzes; Steven Runciman, The Emperor Romanus Lecapenus (1929).

entries.label: Nikephoros II Phokas
entries.hint: Nikephoros Phokas, scion of a Cappadocian family of generals, took Crete in 961, was proclaimed emperor by his army in 963 and married Romanos II's widow Theophano. He conquered Cilicia and Cyprus and in 969 recovered Antioch. He was stern and parsimonious and was murdered by Theophano and John Tzimiskes.
entries.note: Leo the Deacon, History 1–5; Skylitzes; Treadgold 1997.

entries.label: John I Tzimiskes
entries.hint: John Tzimiskes, a general from an Armenian family in Hierapolis, killed Nikephoros in 969, defeated the Rus prince Sviatoslav in Bulgaria in 971 and in 974–975 led a great campaign through Syria. He moved Paulicians to Thrace. He died in 976, perhaps by poison.
entries.note: Leo the Deacon 6–10; Skylitzes; Gustave Schlumberger, L'épopée byzantine (1896–1905).

entries.label: Basil II
entries.hint: Basil II, the 'Bulgar-slayer', put down the revolts of Skleros and Phokas with Russian Varangian troops, took Bulgaria in a thirty-year war, annexed the Armenian and Georgian lands in the East and passed a land law against the great estates. He left the empire at its largest and richest since the seventh century, and a full treasury.
entries.note: Michael Psellos, Chronographia 1; Skylitzes; Catherine Holmes, Basil II and the Governance of Empire (2005).

entries.group: The Last Macedonians and the Doukai
entries.label: The heirs of Basil II
entries.hint: After Basil's death his brother Constantine VIII, then Zoe and her husbands — Romanos III, Michael IV, Michael V and Constantine IX Monomachos — and the empress Theodora ruled in a court of rivalries and civil bureaucrats. The army was neglected and the gold was debased; the annexation of Ani in 1045 was the last territorial gain.
entries.note: Michael Psellos, Chronographia 2–6; Skylitzes; Treadgold 1997.

entries.group: The Last Macedonians and the Doukai
entries.label: Isaac Komnenos to Romanos Diogenes
entries.hint: Isaac I Komnenos, an army candidate, took the throne in 1057 and tried to restore the army, but fell ill and gave way to Constantine X Doukas, who cut military spending. His widow Eudokia married the general Romanos Diogenes, a Cappadocian magnate, in 1068, who went to the East to meet the Seljuks and was beaten at Manzikert in 1071.
entries.note: Psellos, Chronographia 7; Attaleiates, History; Skylitzes continuatus.

entries.label: The Anatolian military aristocracy
entries.hint: The Phokas, Skleros, Maleinos, Doukas, Argyros and Komnenos families held command of the border themes and vast estates in Cappadocia and Pontus. From the tenth century they produced emperors and rebels. Their grip on the army and on the land was the central problem of the Macedonian emperors.
entries.note: Jean-Claude Cheynet, Pouvoir et contestations à Byzance (1990); Alexander Kazhdan, The Aristocracy of Byzantium (1974).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The fall of Tephrike, Kourkouas and Phokas in the East, the revolts of the generals, the Armenian annexations and the road to Manzikert

entries.label: Manzikert
entries.hint: Romanos Diogenes led a large, mixed army to Armenia, split his force, and at Manzikert met the sultan Alp Arslan's smaller army. Betrayal by the rear guard under Andronikos Doukas, a rival, and a feigned retreat lost the day, and the emperor was captured. The Seljuks' terms were mild, but the Byzantine civil war that followed left Anatolia open.
entries.note: Attaleiates, History 18–19; Psellos, Chronographia 7; Alexander Beihammer, Byzantium and the Emergence of Muslim-Turkish Anatolia (2017).

entries.label: The end of Tephrike
entries.hint: Basil I's armies defeated the Paulician leader Chrysocheir at Bathys Ryax in 872 and took Tephrike, ending the sect's state. Chrysocheir's head was brought to the emperor, who is said to have shot an arrow at it. The Paulician danger to western Anatolia ended.
entries.note: Theophanes Continuatus 5.38–41; Peter of Sicily; Garsoïan 1967.

entries.label: The conquests of John Kourkouas
entries.hint: John Kourkouas, domestic of the Scholai for twenty-two years under Romanos I, led annual campaigns across the Euphrates, took Melitene in 934, Samosata and Dvin, and in 944 forced Edessa to hand over the Mandylion. His victories restored the frontier of Cappadocia to the Euphrates.
entries.note: Theophanes Continuatus 6; Skylitzes; Yahya of Antioch; John Haldon, Warfare, State and Society (1999).

entries.label: Nikephoros Phokas in Cilicia and Syria
entries.hint: The Phokas brothers took Aleppo in 962, Nikephoros took Cilicia in 965 — Adana, Mopsuestia and Tarsus — and then Cyprus. Leo Phokas and Peter retook Antioch in October 969, a century after its loss. The conquests pushed the border south of the Taurus.
entries.note: Leo the Deacon 3–5; Skylitzes; Yahya of Antioch; Treadgold 1997.

entries.label: Skleros, Phokas and the revolts of the generals
entries.hint: Bardas Skleros, proclaimed emperor by his army in 976, took most of Anatolia and was defeated by Bardas Phokas in 979. Phokas then rebelled himself in 987 and was beaten and killed at Abydos in 989 when Basil II came with six thousand Rus. The revolts showed that the great families could take the East.
entries.note: Psellos, Chronographia 1; Skylitzes; Holmes 2005.

entries.label: Basil II's wars in Georgia
entries.hint: When David of Tao died in 1000, Basil II claimed his lands and in 1021–1022 invaded Georgia, where the Georgian king Giorgi I fought at Svindax in 1022. Basil won and took Tao and parts of Kartli. The campaigns brought the empire into the Caucasus.
entries.note: Skylitzes; Stephen of Taron; Georgian Chronicles; Holmes 2005.

entries.label: Ani annexed
entries.hint: After the Armenian king Gagik II was forced to cede Ani to Constantine IX Monomachos, the Bagratid capital, a great commercial city of tens of thousands, became a Byzantine province. Its walls had defied the Byzantines for years. The annexation weakened the buffer that had stood between Byzantium and the Turks.
entries.note: Skylitzes; Matthew of Edessa; Aristakes of Lastivert.

entries.label: Kapetron and the Turkmen raids
entries.hint: In 1048 a Seljuk army under Ibrahim Inal and Kutalmish met the Byzantine and Georgian forces at Kapetron in the east, and, though the result was inconclusive, the Turks looted the region of Erzurum. In 1064 Alp Arslan took Ani. The Turkmen horsemen now raided at will.
entries.note: Skylitzes; Aristakes of Lastivert; Matthew of Edessa; Claude Cahen, Pre-Ottoman Turkey (1968).

entries.label: The Turkish raids into the heartland
entries.hint: Turkmen warbands under Seljuk sultans' command reached Caesarea in 1067, Neocaesarea and Amorion in 1068, Iconium in 1069 and Chonae, where they sacked the shrine of the Archangel Michael, in 1070. The themes had been stripped of troops, and the cities were unprepared.
entries.note: Attaleiates, History; Skylitzes continuatus; Michael Psellos, Chronographia 7.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Eparch's Book, the land laws against the powerful, the new border themes and the debased gold

entries.label: The new border themes
entries.hint: Recovering the East, the emperors set up small new themes and frontier commands — Cappadocia, Charsianon, Lykandos, Mesopotamia, Sebasteia — under Armenian and Greek officers with troops from local families. These were units fit to the conditions of Armenian and Syrian settlement.
entries.note: Constantine VII, De thematibus; De administrando imperio; Treadgold 1995.

entries.label: The Book of the Eparch
entries.hint: The Eparch's Book, issued by Leo VI for the city prefect, lists the regulations of the guilds of Constantinople: notaries, jewellers, silk merchants, perfumers, butchers, bakers and others, with their prices, membership and the limits of their trade. It is the best view of the organised economy of a medieval capital.
entries.note: Book of the Eparch, ed. Jules Nicole (1893); trans. Edwin Freshfield (1938); Johannes Koder (1991).

entries.label: The laws against the powerful
entries.hint: In a series of Novels from 922 to 996, Romanos I, Constantine VII and Basil II tried to stop the dynatoi, the powerful, from buying up the lands of peasants and soldiers. Basil's law of 996 abolished the forty-year limit that protected the possessions of the powerful. In 1002 he made the powerful pay the taxes of their neighbours who could not.
entries.note: Novels of Romanos I (922, 934), Constantine VII (947), Basil II (996, 1002); Lemerle, Agrarian History (1979).

entries.label: The debasement of the nomisma
entries.hint: For six centuries the gold coin of Constantinople had held at about 24 carats. From the 1040s under Constantine IX, the gold content was reduced step by step, to some 16 carats by 1070 and then to a third of that. The costly civil administration and the payment of the army were the causes.
entries.note: Michael Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985); Philip Grierson, Byzantine Coinage (1982).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Schism of 1054, the holy mountains, the Mandylion and the transplanted Paulicians

entries.label: The Mandylion comes to Constantinople
entries.hint: As the price for lifting the siege of Edessa, John Kourkouas demanded the Mandylion, a cloth which, according to the story, bore the imprint of Christ's face sent to King Abgar. It was taken in great procession to Constantinople in August 944 and placed in the Pharos chapel. The Church celebrates the day on 16 August.
entries.note: Narratio de imagine Edessena; Skylitzes; Averil Cameron on the image of Edessa.

entries.label: Lazaros of Galesion and the holy mountains
entries.hint: Lazaros, a peasant's son from near Magnesia who became a stylite and then a monastic founder on Mount Galesion near Ephesus, headed a community of monks and had great influence on the people and the great. His Life records the anxieties of the Anatolian countryside as the Turks approached. The holy mountains of Olympus, Latros and Galesion were centres of Anatolian monasticism.
entries.note: Life of Lazaros of Galesion (ed. Richard Greenfield, 2000); Life of Paul of Latros.

entries.label: The Paulicians moved to Thrace
entries.hint: John Tzimiskes resettled Paulicians and Syrian Monophysite Christians from the East near Philippopolis in Thrace to hold the Balkan frontier. In their new home they spread their ideas and, according to some, a dualist heritage that fed the Bogomil movement.
entries.note: Skylitzes; Anna Komnene, Alexiad 14.8–9; Garsoïan 1967.

entries.group: Church of Rome and Eastern Church
entries.label: The Schism of 1054
entries.hint: The papal legate Cardinal Humbert placed a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia in July 1054 against the patriarch Michael Cerularius, who answered with a synod and anathema. The break between the churches of Rome and Constantinople, long in the making, was made. Contemporaries thought it a quarrel of delegates.
entries.note: Humbert, Excommunication of Michael Cerularius (1054); Steven Runciman, The Eastern Schism (1955).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The painted churches of Cappadocia, the Paris Psalter, the frontier epic and the first neumes

entries.label: The painted churches of Cappadocia
entries.hint: In the tenth and eleventh centuries the rock-cut churches of the Göreme valley and its neighbours were painted with whole cycles of the life of Christ and the saints. Tokalı Kilise, the New Church of about 950–960, is the finest, with its lapis blue, and the church of Nikephoros Phokas at Çavuşin was painted in the 960s for the emperor's family.
entries.note: Nicole Thierry, La Cappadoce de l'Antiquité au Moyen Âge (2002); Lyn Rodley (1985); UNESCO World Heritage List no. 357 (Göreme, 1985).

entries.label: The first Byzantine neumes
entries.hint: Systems of signs written above the words of chant appear in Byzantine manuscripts from the ninth century, as reading marks, and from the tenth in the first neumed hymn books (Sticheraria), whose signs recorded melodic movement. The mature Middle Byzantine notation of about 1100 allowed a chant to be sung from the page.
entries.note: Oliver Strunk, Essays on Music in the Byzantine World (1977); Christian Troelsgård, Byzantine Neumes (2011).

entries.label: The Paris Psalter and the Joshua Roll
entries.hint: In the circle of Constantine VII, illuminators made two masterpieces that look back to antiquity: the Paris Psalter, with full-page miniatures of David with personifications in the classical style, and the Joshua Roll, a parchment scroll with a continuous frieze of the conquest of Canaan. They are the best examples of the Macedonian Renaissance.
entries.note: Paris Psalter (BnF gr. 139); Joshua Roll (Vatican, Pal. gr. 431); Kurt Weitzmann, Byzantine Book Illumination and Ivories (1980).

entries.label: Digenes Akrites
entries.hint: The epic of Basil Digenes Akrites, 'the two-born frontiersman', the son of an Arab emir and a Greek woman, tells of the heroes who guarded the border in the days of the Anatolian campaigns, of love, ambushes, the abduction of a bride and raids on the Arabs. Its oldest manuscript is of the twelfth century and it rests on older frontier songs.
entries.note: Digenes Akrites (Grottaferrata and Escorial versions), ed. Elizabeth Jeffreys (1998).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Constantine Porphyrogennetos, Arethas, Leo the Deacon, the Suda and Psellos

entries.label: Arethas of Caesarea
entries.hint: Arethas, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, was a collector who paid for manuscripts of Plato, Euclid, Aristotle, Lucian and Aelius Aristides and annotated them with sharp comments in the margins. The Clarke Plato in Oxford, copied in 895 for him, is among the earliest dated Greek minuscule manuscripts of Plato.
entries.note: Bodleian Library MS E. D. Clarke 39 (Plato, 895); Arethas's scholia; Nigel Wilson, Scholars of Byzantium (1983).

entries.label: Constantine Porphyrogennetos
entries.hint: Constantine VII, born in the purple, had an encyclopaedic programme of books made in the palace: the Book of Ceremonies on court ritual, De administrando imperio, a handbook of foreign policy for his son, De thematibus on the provinces, and a collection of excerpts from historians. The corpus is the empire's self-portrait.
entries.note: Constantine VII, De ceremoniis, De administrando imperio (ed. Moravcsik and Jenkins, 1967), De thematibus (ed. Pertusi, 1952).

entries.label: The Suda
entries.hint: A huge lexicon of some 30,000 entries, the Suda, put together in the late tenth century by unknown compilers, gives definitions of words, biographies of authors and extracts from ancient historians and scholia. It is the largest encyclopaedia of the medieval Greek world.
entries.note: Suda, ed. Ada Adler (1928–38); Suda On Line (Stoa).

entries.label: Leo the Deacon
entries.hint: Leo the Deacon, who was born in Asia Minor and was educated in Constantinople, wrote a history of the reigns of Nikephoros Phokas, John Tzimiskes and the first years of Basil II, as an eyewitness of the campaigns in Bulgaria. He is the best narrator of a high period of conquest.
entries.note: Leo the Deacon, History (ed. Hase, 1828; trans. Alice-Mary Talbot and Denis Sullivan, 2005).

entries.label: Michael Psellos
entries.hint: Michael Psellos, a lawyer and philosopher who served as chief minister under several emperors, wrote the Chronographia, a vivid, frank account of the emperors from Basil II to Michael VII, and hundreds of letters and rhetorical works. He revived the study of Plato and Proclus, and his work is the key to the intellectual life of the eleventh century.
entries.note: Michael Psellos, Chronographia (ed. Impellizzeri, 1984); Letters; Anthony Kaldellis, The Argument of Psellos' Chronographia (1999).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The estates of Maleinos, the recovery of the countryside and the debased nomisma

entries.label: The recovery of the countryside
entries.hint: Under the shelter of the long peace of the interior, villages grew and cities such as Ephesus, Smyrna and Nicaea revived. Land that was fallow in the seventh century came back under the plough and the monasteries gained estates. The population probably rose in the tenth and eleventh centuries.
entries.note: Michael Angold, The Byzantine Empire 1025–1204 (1984); Lemerle 1979.

entries.label: Eustathios Maleinos and the great estates
entries.hint: Eustathios Maleinos, a Cappadocian magnate, was so rich that when Basil II marched through his estates, he feasted the whole army and its baggage train, and the emperor, alarmed, kept him in Constantinople till he died and took his lands. The anecdote is told in chronicles as the symbol of the power of the great landowners.
entries.note: Skylitzes; Psellos, Chronographia 1.29; Kekaumenos, Strategikon.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The cross-in-square church and the manuals of frontier war

entries.label: The cross-in-square church
entries.hint: Basil I's Nea Ekklesia, built in 880, gave the standard form of the middle Byzantine church: a small square with four columns carrying a central dome and four barrel vaults forming a cross, with three apses. The form fitted the monastic and aristocratic churches of the Anatolian plateau.
entries.note: Photius, Homily 10 (on the Nea); Constantine VII, Vita Basilii; Cyril Mango, Byzantine Architecture (1976).

entries.label: The manuals of frontier war
entries.hint: Leo VI's Taktika, the Praecepta militaria of Nikephoros Phokas and the anonymous De velitatione bellica on shadowing raiders describe the army's formations, the heavy cavalry, the cataphract wedge, camps, signals and the tactics against Arab raids. They reflect the experience of frontier war in Anatolia.
entries.note: Leo VI, Taktika; Nikephoros Phokas, Praecepta militaria; De velitatione bellica, ed. George Dennis, Three Byzantine Military Treatises (1985).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Vladimir's baptism, the truce with the Fatimids, the Armenian cessions and the privileges of Venice

entries.label: The marriage of Anna and the baptism of Vladimir
entries.hint: In return for six thousand Rus soldiers for his civil war, Basil II agreed to give his sister Anna in marriage to Vladimir of Kiev, who accepted baptism. The Varangian Guard formed from those troops became the emperor's bodyguard. The conversion made Rus a part of the Orthodox world.
entries.note: Russian Primary Chronicle (s.a. 6496); Yahya of Antioch; Skylitzes; Dimitri Obolensky, The Byzantine Commonwealth (1971).

entries.label: The chrysobull of 992 for Venice
entries.hint: Basil II granted Venetian merchants reduced customs duties in Constantinople and the right of passage in return for naval service. The act is the earliest great trade privilege for the Italian republics, which would in the later eleventh century and the twelfth turn Byzantine ports into their domain.
entries.note: Chrysobull of 992 (Tafel and Thomas, Urkunden); Donald Nicol, Byzantium and Venice (1988).

entries.label: The truce with the Fatimids
entries.hint: After the Fatimid victories over the Byzantine forces at Apamea in 998, Basil II and the caliph al-Hakim agreed in 1001 a ten-year truce, the first of a series. It left the Byzantines free to wage war in Bulgaria and the Caucasus.
entries.note: Yahya of Antioch; Skylitzes; Marius Canard's studies of Fatimid–Byzantine relations.

entries.label: Senekerim and Vaspurakan
entries.hint: Facing pressure from the Seljuks, the Armenian king Senekerim Artsruni of Vaspurakan ceded his kingdom to Basil II in return for lands in Cappadocia around Sebasteia. About 14,000 Armenians moved with him. Armenian settlement in Anatolia rose, and Vaspurakan became a Byzantine theme.
entries.note: Aristakes of Lastivert 2; Matthew of Edessa; Skylitzes.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The border moved east, the earthquake of 989, the Turkmen and the army that was dismissed

entries.label: The frontier moved to the Euphrates
entries.hint: In a century the border moved from the Taurus passes to the Euphrates, to northern Syria and to the Caucasus. The Cappadocian and Armenian lands were Byzantine again, and Antioch and Edessa with them. The frontier zone was settled by Armenians and Syrians.
entries.note: Treadgold 1997; Holmes 2005.

entries.label: The earthquake of 989
entries.hint: On 25 October 989 a quake brought down part of the dome of Hagia Sophia. Basil II asked the Armenian architect Trdat of Ani, the builder of the cathedral of Ani, to repair it, and the work was done by 994. The disaster shows the empire's use of Armenian skill.
entries.note: Yahya of Antioch; Leo the Deacon 10.10; Mainstone, Hagia Sophia (1988).

entries.label: The Turkmen arrive
entries.hint: The Oghuz Turkmen, moving west before the Seljuk conquests of Iran, came into Armenia and Azerbaijan from the 1020s and raided the Byzantine East in groups. Their herds needed pastures and the empire's frontier was thin. The region was changed within fifty years.
entries.note: Claude Cahen, Pre-Ottoman Turkey (1968); Beihammer 2017.

entries.label: The army that was dismissed
entries.hint: After the annexations the East was under-garrisoned: Constantine IX disbanded the army of Iberia (some 50,000 men, by Attaleiates' figure) and taxed the soldiers instead. The decision saved money and gave the Turks the Armenian marches. The effect on the defence of the East is debated.
entries.note: Attaleiates, History 5; Skylitzes continuatus; Psellos, Chronographia 6.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Zoe and Theodora, the eunuch Basil and the frontier of the Akritai

entries.label: The frontier of the Akritai
entries.hint: In the border districts lived the akritai, soldier-farmers who kept the passes and made raids, in a mixed society of Greeks, Armenians, Syrians and Arabs who intermarried and traded across the line. The border was a zone of its own, with its own heroes and songs. The De velitatione describes their way of life.
entries.note: De velitatione bellica (ed. Dennis 1985); Digenes Akrites.

entries.label: Basil the Parakoimomenos
entries.hint: Basil Lekapenos, an illegitimate son of Romanos I by a Russian slave, was castrated as a child and rose to be chamberlain, minister and the real power in the state under four emperors. He built a great monastery and church, had the finest manuscripts made, and Basil II removed him in 985.
entries.note: Skylitzes; Psellos 1; Leo the Deacon; Kathryn Ringrose, The Perfect Servant (2003).

entries.label: Zoe and Theodora
entries.hint: Zoe, daughter of Constantine VIII and the last porphyrogenita except Theodora, was empress through three husbands and in 1042 shared the throne with her sister Theodora in a rare joint rule of two women. After Zoe's death Theodora ruled alone, 1055–1056, as sole emperor in her seventies.
entries.note: Psellos, Chronographia 3–6; Judith Herrin, Women in Purple (2001).
